slides.title: Fission + the nuclear reaction
slides.body:
**Nuclear fission**: heavy nucleus (U-235, Pu-239) absorbs a neutron + splits into two lighter nuclei + 2-3 neutrons + ~200 MeV energy.

Key: each fission releases NEUTRONS that can trigger MORE fissions → **chain reaction**.

**Critical mass**: minimum amount of fissile material to sustain a chain reaction. Depends on:
- Enrichment level (U-235 fraction; natural U is 0.7%, reactor fuel 3-5%, weapons-grade >90%).
- Geometry (spherical = lowest critical mass).
- Neutron moderator presence.
- Surrounding material (reflector).

**Neutron moderation**: fast (fission-energy ~2 MeV) neutrons are inefficient at causing more fissions. Slow them via collisions with light elements:
- Water (H₂O): hydrogen is best moderator. Standard.
- Heavy water (D₂O): D less absorbing than H → enables natural U fuel (CANDU).
- Graphite (C): solid moderator. RBMK (Chernobyl), Magnox.
- Sodium, helium, lead: 'fast' reactors (no moderation).

**Multiplication factor** $k$:
- $k < 1$: subcritical. Reaction dies out.
- $k = 1$: critical. Sustained reaction. STEADY STATE = reactor operation.
- $k > 1$: supercritical. Power increases. WEAPONS or runaway accident.

**Control rods**: absorb neutrons (B, Cd, Hf). Insert to reduce reactivity, withdraw to increase. Maintain $k = 1$ during normal operation.

**Delayed neutrons**: ~0.65% of fissions emit neutrons after seconds (vs ~$10^{-13}$ s for prompt neutrons). These provide TIMING MARGIN for control. Reactor operates 'prompt subcritical, delayed critical'.

**Fission energy distribution**:
- ~80% kinetic energy of fragments (heat).
- ~5% prompt neutrons.
- ~5% prompt gammas.
- ~10% beta + gamma from decay of fission products (waste heat AFTER shutdown).

The decay-heat tail is why Fukushima failed despite shutdown — pumps stopped + no cooling for the post-shutdown heat → meltdown.

slides.title: Reactor types + generations
slides.body:
**Generation I** (1950s-60s): early experimental + commercial. Shippingport, Calder Hall. Retired.

**Generation II** (~70s-90s, currently most operating reactors):
- **PWR (Pressurized Water Reactor)**: most common (~60% globally). Water moderator + coolant, pressurized to stay liquid at 300+°C. AP1000, EPR.
- **BWR (Boiling Water Reactor)**: water boils in core directly. GE designs. ~20%.
- **PHWR (CANDU)**: heavy water moderator + natural U fuel. Canadian.
- **AGR**: gas-cooled, graphite-moderated. UK.
- **RBMK**: graphite-moderated + water-cooled. Soviet design; Chernobyl's type.
- **VVER**: Soviet/Russian PWR. ~10%.

**Generation III + III+** (active deployment): improved safety + economics.
- **AP1000** (Westinghouse): passive safety systems (no power needed for emergency cooling).
- **EPR** (Framatome): high power (1.6+ GW), defense-in-depth.
- **APR1400** (KEPCO Korea): exports to UAE, operating.
- **VVER-1200** (Rosatom): Russian flagship.
- **HPR1000** (China): two-loop design.

**Generation IV** (in development): radical changes.
- **Small Modular Reactors (SMRs)**: <300 MW. Factory-built. NuScale (USA), GE Hitachi BWRX-300, X-energy Xe-100, Rolls-Royce SMR. Faster to deploy + lower upfront cost.
- **Sodium-cooled fast reactors**: Russian BN-800 operating. France SUPERPHENIX retired. India PFBR.
- **High-temperature gas-cooled** (HTGR, VHTR): efficient, can produce process heat for hydrogen.
- **Molten salt reactors (MSR)**: ThorCon, Terrestrial Energy, Moltex. Liquid fuel. Thorium-fueled variants possible.
- **Lead-cooled**: heavy + corrosive but no positive coid coefficient.

**Reactor lifecycle**:
- Fuel: enrich U-235 to 3-5%, fabricate into pellets + rods.
- Operation: 1-2 year fuel cycles. Refueling outage 30-90 days.
- Spent fuel: cool in pool 5-10 years; then dry cask storage; eventually deep geologic repository (Onkalo, Finland operational 2025+).

**Reactor lifecycle from cradle to grave** is well-studied; total life-cycle CO₂ ~10-15 g/kWh, comparable to wind + solar (and far below gas at ~400+ or coal 800+).

slides.title: Safety + waste + fusion
slides.body:
**Nuclear safety**: high consequences, very low probability.

**Accidents**:
- **Three Mile Island (1979)**: PWR partial meltdown. Operator confusion + indicators. Reactor lost but radiation release small. Public concern + USA construction halt.
- **Chernobyl (1986)**: RBMK reactor explosion. Design flaws (positive void coefficient, no containment), botched safety test, secrecy. ~30 immediate deaths; ~4,000 estimated long-term cancers. Major release into Europe.
- **Fukushima Daiichi (2011)**: BWR. Tsunami flooded backup diesels. Cooling lost. Three reactors melted. Hydrogen explosions. No radiation deaths from incident; significant economic damage + cleanup ongoing. Japan shut down nuclear for years.

**Modern safety architecture** (Gen III+):
- **Passive cooling**: physics-based (gravity, convection) emergency systems. Don't need power or active intervention. AP1000 + EPR exemplify.
- **Defense in depth**: multiple independent layers of protection.
- **Probabilistic Risk Assessment (PRA)**: identify + quantify failure pathways.
- **Severe accident management**: contain even worst-case meltdowns.

**Waste**:
- High-level waste (HLW): spent fuel. Tiny volume (per kWh) but very long-lived (10,000+ years to natural background).
- Geologic disposal: Yucca Mountain stalled (USA). Finland's Onkalo operating. Sweden Forsmark approved. Most countries: spent fuel in dry casks, awaiting repository.
- Some fuel can be reprocessed (extract Pu + U for re-use). France does this. USA does not (proliferation concerns).

**Fusion**:
- **D-T fusion**: deuterium + tritium → helium + neutron + 17.6 MeV.
- 4× more energy per nucleon than fission.
- No long-lived waste; tritium short-lived; activated structural materials moderate.
- No criticality risk.
- Fuel: D from seawater (essentially inexhaustible). T bred from Li in blanket.
- Hot enough that no material can contain → magnetic confinement (tokamak, stellarator) or inertial (laser).

**Status**: 
- **ITER (Cadarache, France)**: international tokamak. First plasma ~2025 (delayed). Q ~ 10 target (10× energy output vs input). Full operation ~2035.
- **NIF (USA)**: laser inertial. December 2022 + repeated 2023-24: ignition (Q > 1 in fusion reaction; not net energy when including laser power).
- **Private fusion**: Commonwealth Fusion, TAE Technologies, Helion, Tokamak Energy, others. Billions raised. Targeting net energy in 2030s.
- 'Fusion is 20 years away' — joke. Progress is real but COMMERCIAL fusion still ~2040+.

**Nuclear's renewable role**: zero-carbon, baseload, dense. Complement to variable renewables. Growth pathways: SMRs, lifetime extensions of existing fleet, new builds in China + India + UAE + Korea. Future: fusion if commercial.

question.question: Estimate energy from a reactor
question.goal: 1000 MW thermal nuclear reactor, 33% thermal-to-electric efficiency, capacity factor 92%. Annual electricity output? Compare to a 1000 MW solar plant at CF 25%.

steps.prompt: Same capacity, different annual energy. Reactor produces ~20% more energy than equivalent-capacity solar despite smaller electrical rating. Why?

options: Capacity factor: nuclear 92% (baseload) vs solar 25% (variable). The reactor's high availability per year compensates for lower nameplate. Compare 'energy per nameplate W' to fairly evaluate.

steps.reveal: Nuclear's 92% capacity factor (vs solar 25%) means ~3.7× more energy per nameplate watt. But solar PV is much cheaper per nameplate (\$1/W vs \$5-10/W for nuclear) so the economics depend on weighing capacity vs energy delivery. Both have roles in a decarbonized grid.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{Energy} = P_{rated} \cdot 8760 \cdot CF}$$ Nuclear's high capacity factor (~92%) makes it competitive on energy delivery despite higher capex. Solar's lower capex but lower CF means more nameplate needed for same energy. Optimal mix in a decarbonized grid depends on demand patterns + storage costs + technology mix. Most planners see roles for both, complementing.

question.question: Why is fusion still 'always 30 years away' even after the 2022 NIF ignition breakthrough?
options: Ignition (Q > 1) at NIF means net fusion energy at the level of the fusion reaction. NOT net energy when accounting for laser inefficiency (Q ~150 needed for net plant energy). Tokamak fusion needs continuous operation, materials for years of neutron flux, tritium breeding, all unsolved. Commercial fusion power plants are still ~2040+ best estimate.
question.explanation:
NIF's December 2022 breakthrough: input ~2 MJ laser energy yielded 3 MJ fusion energy. But total LASER energy was ~300 MJ (lasers ~1% efficient). So plant-level Q ~0.01. For commercial fusion, plant-level Q ~10 needed. Plus: tokamak fusion needs continuous (vs NIF's pulsed) operation; structural materials must survive years of 14 MeV neutron flux; tritium must be bred in lithium blankets at sustainable rates. All UNSOLVED engineering challenges. Best estimates: commercial fusion ~2040-2050 if everything goes well. The 'always 30 years' joke reflects real engineering complexity rather than scientific impossibility.

That said: private fusion (CFS, Helion, TAE, Tokamak Energy) targeting earlier dates with novel approaches.

slides.workedSolution: NIF: Q_reaction > 1 (3 MJ out / 2 MJ laser in to capsule). But lasers ~1% efficient → plant Q ~0.01. Need plant Q ~10 for commercial. Plus: continuous operation, neutron-resistant materials, tritium breeding, all in 30+ year R&D. Best estimate: commercial fusion ~2040-2050. Private fusion targeting earlier. Real but engineering-bounded, not 'always 30 years away'.

Small modular reactors
question.prompt: An SMR developer pitches 100 MW reactors deployed in factories. Walk through why SMRs might (or might not) revive nuclear power.
Explain in two or three sentences why nuclear power is uniquely positioned as a clean-energy source despite public concerns.
question.rubric: Mentions that nuclear provides high-density, dispatchable, zero-carbon baseload power; capacity factors 90%+ + life cycle emissions comparable to wind/solar; major concerns (safety, waste, cost) are real but recent designs + SMRs address some. Most decarbonization scenarios (IPCC, IEA) require nuclear in the mix; without it, solar + wind + storage + transmission needs are dramatically larger + more expensive.
